findings.title: CVE-2026-123039 — Check Point Multiple Products Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource Vulnerability
findings.summary: Vendor: Check Point | Product: Multiple Products. Check Point Firewall, Multi-Domain Security Management Server, Scalable Platforms, Security Gateway, and Security Management Server contain an incorrect permissions assignment for critical resources vulnerability when the Gaia OS DynamicCLI daemon runs as root and listens on a world-writable local socket without authenticating connecting processes. An authenticated local user can send a command to the socket and have it executed as root. Required action: Apply mitigations in accordance with vendor instructions, ensuring compliance with CISA’s BOD 26-04 Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk (see URL in Notes) guidance and CISA’s “Forensics Triage Requirements” (see URL in Notes). Follow applicable BOD 26-04 guidance for cloud services or discontinue use of the product if mitigations are unavailable. Stakeholders are responsible for evaluating each asset's internet exposure and ensuring adherence to BOD 26-04 patching guidelines. (due 2026-11-16)

findings.title: AI threats in the wild: The current state of prompt injections on the web
findings.summary: Posted by Thomas Brunner, Yu-Han Liu, Moni Pande At Google, our Threat Intelligence teams are dedicated to staying ahead of real-world adversarial activity, proactively monitoring emerging threats before they can impact users. Right now, Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) is a top priority for the security community, anticipating it as a primary attack vector for adversaries to target and compromise AI agents. But while the danger of IPI is widely discussed, are threat actors actually exploiting this vector today – and if so, how? To answer these questions and to uncover real-world abuse, we initiated a broad sweep of the public web to monitor for known indirect prompt injection patterns. This is what we found. The threat of indirect prompt injection Unlike a direct injection where a user "jailbreaks" a chatbot, IPI occurs when an AI system processes content—like a website, email, or document—that contains malicious instructions. When the AI reads this poisoned content, it may silently follow the attacker's commands instead of the user's original intent. This is not a new area of concern for us and Google has been working tirelessly to combat these threats. Our efforts involve cross-functional collaboration between researchers at Google DeepMind (GDM) and defenders like the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG). We have previously detailed our work in this area and researchers have further highlighted the evolving nature of these vulnerabilities. Despite this collective focus, a fundamental question remains: to what degree are real-world malicious actors currently operationalizing these attacks? Proactive monitoring at Google The landscape of IPI on the web There are many channels through which attackers might try to send prompt injections. However, one location is particularly easy to observe - the public web. Here, threat actors may simply seed prompt injections on websites in hope of corrupting AI systems that browse them. findings.title: Google Workspace’s continuous approach to mitigating indirect prompt injections
findings.summary: Posted by Adam Gavish, Google GenAI Security Team Indirect prompt injection (IPI) is an evolving threat vector targeting users of complex AI applications with multiple data sources, such as Workspace with Gemini. This technique enables the attacker to influence the behavior of an LLM by injecting malicious instructions into the data or tools used by the LLM as it completes the user’s query. This may even be possible without any input directly from the user. IPI is not the kind of technical problem you “solve” and move on. Sophisticated LLMs with increasing use of agentic automation combined with a wide range of content create an ultra-dynamic and evolving playground for adversarial attacks. That’s why Google takes a sophisticated and comprehensive approach to these attacks. We’re continuously improving LLM resistance to IPI attacks and launching AI application capabilities with ever-improving defenses. Staying ahead of the latest indirect prompt injection attacks is critical to our mission of securing Workspace with Gemini. In our previous blog “ Mitigating prompt injection attacks with a layered defense strategy ”, we reviewed the layered architecture of our IPI defenses. In this blog, we’ll share more detail on the continuous approach we take to improve these defenses and to solve for new attacks. Specialized teams execute attacks based on realistic user profiles to exploit weaknesses, coordinating with product teams to resolve identified issues. findings.title: Architecting Security for Agentic Capabilities in Chrome
findings.summary: Posted by Nathan Parker, Chrome security team Chrome has been advancing the web’s security for well over 15 years, and we’re committed to meeting new challenges and opportunities with AI. Billions of people trust Chrome to keep them safe by default, and this is a responsibility we take seriously. Following the recent launch of Gemini in Chrome and the preview of agentic capabilities , we want to share our approach and some new innovations to improve the safety of agentic browsing. The primary new threat facing all agentic browsers is indirect prompt injection . It can appear in malicious sites, third-party content in iframes, or from user-generated content like user reviews, and can cause the agent to take unwanted actions such as initiating financial transactions or exfiltrating sensitive data. Given this open challenge, we are investing in a layered defense that includes both deterministic and probabilistic defenses to make it difficult and costly for attackers to cause harm. Designing safe agentic browsing for Chrome has involved deep collaboration of security experts across Google. We built on Gemini's existing protections and agent security principles and have implemented several new layers for Chrome. We’re introducing a user alignment critic where the agent’s actions are vetted by a separate model that is isolated from untrusted content. We’re also extending Chrome’s origin-isolation capabilities to constrain what origins the agent can interact with, to just those that are relevant to the task. Our layered defense also includes user confirmations for critical steps, real-time detection of threats , and red-teaming and response . We’ll step through these layers below. findings.title: Rust in Android: move fast and fix things
findings.summary: Posted by Jeff Vander Stoep, Android Last year, we wrote about why a memory safety strategy that focuses on vulnerability prevention in new code quickly yields durable and compounding gains. This year we look at how this approach isn’t just fixing things, but helping us move faster . The 2025 data continues to validate the approach, with memory safety vulnerabilities falling below 20% of total vulnerabilities for the first time. Updated data for 2025. This data covers first-party and third-party (open source) code changes to the Android platform across C, C++, Java, Kotlin, and Rust. This post is published a couple of months before the end of 2025, but Android’s industry-standard 90-day patch window means that these results are very likely close to final. We can and will accelerate patching when necessary. We adopted Rust for its security and are seeing a 1000x reduction in memory safety vulnerability density compared to Android’s C and C++ code . But the biggest surprise was Rust's impact on software delivery. With Rust changes having a 4x lower rollback rate and spending 25% less time in code review , the safer path is now also the faster one. In this post, we dig into the data behind this shift and also cover: How we’re expanding our reach: We're pushing to make secure code the default across our entire software stack. We have updates on Rust adoption in first-party apps, the Linux kernel, and firmware. findings.title: Mitigating prompt injection attacks with a layered defense strategy
findings.summary: Posted by Adam Gavish, Google GenAI Security Team With the rapid adoption of generative AI, a new wave of threats is emerging across the industry with the aim of manipulating the AI systems themselves. One such emerging attack vector is indirect prompt injections. Unlike direct prompt injections, where an attacker directly inputs malicious commands into a prompt, indirect prompt injections involve hidden malicious instructions within external data sources. These may include emails, documents, or calendar invites that instruct AI to exfiltrate user data or execute other rogue actions. As more governments, businesses, and individuals adopt generative AI to get more done, this subtle yet potentially potent attack becomes increasingly pertinent across the industry, demanding immediate attention and robust security measures. At Google, our teams have a longstanding precedent of investing in a defense-in-depth strategy, including robust evaluation, threat analysis, AI security best practices , AI red-teaming , adversarial training, and model hardening for generative AI tools. This approach enables safer adoption of Gemini in Google Workspace and the Gemini app (we refer to both in this blog as “Gemini” for simplicity). Below we describe our prompt injection mitigation product strategy based on extensive research, development, and deployment of improved security mitigations. A layered security approach Google has taken a layered security approach introducing security measures designed for each stage of the prompt lifecycle. From Gemini 2.5 model hardening, to purpose-built machine learning (ML) models detecting malicious instructions, to system-level safeguards, we are meaningfully elevating the difficulty, expense, and complexity faced by an attacker. This approach compels adversaries to resort to methods that are either more easily identified or demand greater resources. findings.summary: Russian State-Supported Cyber Actors Conduct Phishing Campaign Targeting Users of Zimbra Collaboration Suite Executive summary A group of Russian state-supported cyber actors has been targeting and compromising various Western government and commercial organizations using the Zimbra Collaboration Suite (ZCS) software since at least July 2025. The Russian state-supported advanced persistent threat (APT) group’s activity is tracked in the cybersecurity community under several names (see Cybersecurity industry tracking ), primarily as “LAUNDRY BEAR,” a name initially coined by the Netherlands General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) and Defence Intelligence and Security Service (MIVD) [ 1 ]. LAUNDRY BEAR’s targeting is almost certainly to gather sensitive information for the Russian Federation, with these actors primarily focusing on the covert acquisition of email data. Previous campaigns indicated LAUNDRY BEAR relied on unsophisticated initial access techniques—including password spraying, phishing, and pass-the-cookie—allowing the group to successfully run high-volume operations. The latest campaign targeting ZCS uses a novel exploit that was a zero-day vulnerability when first exploited and continues to be successfully exploited. The vulnerability, Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) CVE-2025-66376 , was patched in November 2025. This demonstrates LAUNDRY BEAR’s intent and ability to deploy increasingly sophisticated technical capabilities. Unlike traditional phishing campaigns that persuade a user into taking an action, such as clicking a link or opening a file, LAUNDRY BEAR’s latest campaign leverages a view-based exploit that only requires a user to view a malicious email within a vulnerable version of the webmail service. findings.title: Nuxt: Incomplete fix for GHSA-9v7c-q64q-vv33: a leading `//` in the request path bypasses `server/middleware` path checks and server route rules on page routes
findings.summary:
### Summary

Since `4.6.0`, Nuxt parses a request path that starts with `//` as a URL with a host before rendering a page, so `//x/admin` renders the page at `/admin`. Nitro's routing, Nitro's route rules and `server/middleware` see the path as `//x/admin`, so server-side checks keyed on `/admin` do not apply. The fix for [GHSA-9v7c-q64q-vv33](https://github.com/nuxt/nuxt/security/advisories/GHSA-9v7c-q64q-vv33) in `4.6.3` covered dot segments but not this form.

### Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can bypass server-side controls that match on the request path of a page route.

A route-scoped server handler is skipped:

```ts
// nuxt.config.ts
export default defineNuxtConfig({
  serverHandlers: [{ route: '/admin', middleware: true, handler: '~~/server/admin-guard.ts' }],
})
```

```ts
// server/admin-guard.ts
export default defineEventHandler((event) => {
  if (!isAuthenticated(event)) {
    throw createError({ statusCode: 401 })
  }
})
```

With this handler, `/admin` returns 401, but `//x/admin` and `///x/admin` render `app/pages/admin.vue` along with the data it fetches during server rendering. `server/middleware` that checks `event.path.startsWith('/admin')` is skipped in the same way.

Server-side `redirect` and `headers` route rules are also skipped, so `'/admin/**': { redirect: '/login' }` does not redirect `//x/admin/secret`, and per-route security headers such as `Content-Security-Policy` are not sent.

Browsers send a path such as `//x/admin` as written, so a plain link is enough to reach the page.

Not affected:

- API handlers in `server/api` and `server/routes`, which Nitro does not match for these paths.
- `appMiddleware` route rules and middleware declared with `definePageMeta`, which are matched against the resolved route.
- Nuxt `3.x` and `4.0.0` to `4.5.x`, which pass the path to the page router unchanged, so these requests 404.

### Patches

Fixed in `@nuxt/nitro-server@4.6.4`, which `nuxt@4.6.4` depends on. The renderer now uses the request p

findings.title: OpenTelemetry JavaScript: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File and Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor in @opentelemetry/instrumentation-http
findings.summary:
### Summary

`@opentelemetry/instrumentation-http` redacts sensitive URL query parameters on **outgoing (client) spans** but not on **incoming (server) spans**. The server-span path writes the raw query string verbatim into the `url.query` attribute, so credentials embedded in inbound request URLs — AWS presigned-URL signatures, Azure SAS tokens (`sig`), GCS signed-URL signatures — are exported in plaintext to the configured tracing backend.

Configuring the `redactedQueryParams` option **does not change this**, as this applies only to outgoing (client) spans.

### Impact

**Information disclosure / credential leakage** (CWE-200; CWE-532, insertion of sensitive information into telemetry data).

**Who is impacted:** any Node.js service instrumented with `@opentelemetry/instrumentation-http` — directly or transitively via `@opentelemetry/auto-instrumentations-node` — that receives inbound requests carrying credentials in the query string. Common cases: services fronting presigned S3/GCS downloads, Azure SAS-token URLs, and signature-authenticated webhooks.

**Consequence:** clients' still-valid credentials are written into server spans and stored by the tracing backend, readable by anyone with span-read access — observability vendor infrastructure, dashboard users, and internal audiences far broader than the credential's intended scope. Presigned-URL signatures typically remain valid for minutes to days after capture, so this is not merely historical exposure.

**Severity:** Moderate. Exploitation requires read access to the telemetry backend, and inbound URLs must actually carry signed credentials. However, the gap is a documented mitigation that silently fails to apply, which defeats the mitigation operators would reach for.

### Patches

This vulnerability has been patched in `@opentelemetry/instrumentation-http` version `0.222.0`.
Known sensitive query string values (as defined by Semantic Conventions) are redacted by default from span data for incoming spans.

findings.title: Astro: Image endpoint in @astrojs/node can read files from a case-variant sibling of the output directory on case-sensitive filesystems
findings.summary:
## Summary

The `/_image` endpoint used by the `@astrojs/node` adapter checks that a requested local image is inside the build output directory before reading it from disk. That check compared paths case-insensitively. On case-sensitive filesystems (such as Linux), a directory whose path differs from the output directory only by letter case is a different directory, but it passed the check.

For example, with the client output directory at `/srv/app/dist/client/`, a request such as:

```text
/_image?href=/../../DIST/client/secret.png&w=32&f=png
```

resolved to `/srv/app/DIST/client/secret.png` and was served, even though that file is outside the output directory.

## Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can read image files from outside the output directory, but only when all of the following are true:

- The site uses on-demand rendering with the `@astrojs/node` adapter.
- The server runs on a case-sensitive filesystem.
- A directory exists whose path matches the output directory except for letter case (for example `DIST/client` next to `dist/client`). Such a layout is unusual, and the attacker cannot create it.

Only files the image service accepts can be read. Raster images are returned after resizing; SVG files are returned unchanged. Other file types fail during processing. Plain path traversal outside the output directory (for example `/../../secret.png`) was already rejected and is not affected.

## Affected versions

`astro` >= 5.14.3, <= 7.4.6, when used with `@astrojs/node` (all versions up to 11.1.11). The vulnerable image endpoint is provided by `astro` and used by the `@astrojs/node` adapter.

## Patches

Fixed in `astro` 7.4.7. The path check now compares paths exactly, and only ignores letter case for Windows drive-letter paths. The fix ships in `astro`, so upgrading `@astrojs/node` alone is not enough.

## Workarounds

Upgrade to `astro` 7.4.7 or later. Before upgrading, make sure no directory next to the build output directory has a path that differ

findings.title: rails-html-sanitizer: Possible XSS via shared scrubber state in concurrent calls
findings.summary:
## Summary

`Rails::HTML::SafeListSanitizer` (both the HTML4 and HTML5 variants) shares one `Rails::HTML::PermitScrubber` across every `sanitize` call on the same instance, assigning its `tags` and `attributes` on each call without synchronization. Two concurrent `sanitize` calls with different `tags:` or `attributes:` options can interleave, so one call is scrubbed with the other call's allowlist.

- Versions affected: `< 1.7.2`
- Not affected: none
- Fixed versions: `1.7.2`

## Impact

Action View memoizes a single `SafeListSanitizer` per helper module and uses it for every `sanitize` call in the process, so in a multi-threaded server (for example Puma) all requests share the same `PermitScrubber`. If any code path calls `sanitize` with a more permissive allowlist, an attacker who can trigger that path concurrently with another request can cause the other request to be sanitized with the permissive allowlist. If the permissive allowlist admits `script` or an event-handler attribute, the strict call emits it unchanged, which is a cross-site scripting vector when the strict output is stored or rendered to other users.

Applications are affected only if they run more than one thread per process and some `sanitize` call passes `tags:` or `attributes:` options that differ from another call's, including a call that passes no options and so uses the defaults. Applications that use a single configuration everywhere, pass their own `scrubber:`, or run single-threaded are not affected.

## Workarounds

Use the same allowlist for every `sanitize` call, or pass a `scrubber:` built per call (`Rails::HTML::PermitScrubber.new` with `tags=` and `attributes=` set) instead of `tags:` and `attributes:` options.

## Credit

Reported by hiumee via HackerOne.

findings.title: Active Storage: Possible arbitrary file write and read in image analysis
findings.summary:
### Impact
A Rails application that processes attachments with ImageMagick may allow an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files on the server and, when attachments are stored with the Disk service, to read arbitrary files readable by the application process. Those files typically include `secret_key_base` and credentials for external systems, which may in turn allow escalation to remote code execution or lateral movement to those systems.

### Details
ImageMagick selects a coder from the content of the file it is given, and some coders act on files named inside the image rather than on the image itself. Active Storage constrained none of ImageMagick's coders, and the ImageMagick analyzer runs when a file is attached, so an attacker who can upload a crafted file may be able to invoke one. Attaching the upload is sufficient; no variant, preview, or `analyze` call is required. One specific attack chain has been reported to us, but we do not assume it is the only one that exists.

The fixed versions ship an ImageMagick security policy and prepend its directory to `MAGICK_CONFIGURE_PATH` through `MiniMagick.cli_env`, so every ImageMagick process that MiniMagick spawns applies it. The policy denies the `MSL` scripting coder, the coders that read or delete files other than the image, fetch remote or local references, or display to a screen, every coder backed by Ghostscript together with the `gs` delegate, and `@filename` indirection. ImageMagick applies every `policy.xml` on its search path, so the shipped policy adds to the host's policy rather than replacing it. The policy applies to every ImageMagick command that MiniMagick runs, not only those of Active Storage. See the `activestorage` CHANGELOG and "ImageMagick Security Policy" in the Active Storage guide.

- Uses ImageMagick for Active Storage image processing. This is `config.active_storage.variant_processor = :min

### Impact
When `ActionDispatch::Cookies` reads a signed or encrypted cookie that was written under a rotated secret (`config.action_dispatch.cookies_rotations`) or in the format that a `:hybrid` cookie serializer migrates from, it writes the cookie back to the response in the current format, and that write ignores `request.session_options[:skip]`. `ActiveStorage::DisableSession` relies on that option to keep the session cookie off the public, immutable responses of the Active Storage proxy controllers, but those controllers still load the session, so a request carrying an old-format session cookie could receive the rewritten session cookie in `Set-Cookie` on a cacheable response. A shared cache that stores such a response together with its `Set-Cookie` header could then serve one user's session to later requesters of the same URL, or serve an attacker's session to other users.

Applications are affected when they serve Active Storage files through the proxy controllers, have a cookie rotation or a `:hybrid` serializer migration configured, and run behind a cache that stores `Set-Cookie` on public responses. This is a path around the fix for [CVE-2024-26144](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8h22-8cf7-hq6g).

### Details
In the fixed releases, a response that skips the session leaves an old-format signed or encrypted cookie unchanged, and the next request that does not skip the session upgrades it. An application that skips the session on every request no longer upgrades its signed or encrypted cookies. Cookies that the application sets explicitly are still written. See the Action Pack CHANGELOG.

### Workarounds
Configure caching proxies not to store responses that carry a `Set-Cookie` header, or complete the cookie rotation or serializer migration and remove it from the configuration.

### Releases
The fixed releases are available at the normal locations.

Patches for those who cannot upgrade at once:
- 8.1: https://github.com/rails/rails/commit/849a6c30eacbb6ca4

findings.title: Pillow: Memory DoS in TIFF and EXIF IFD parsing via overlapping tag data
findings.summary:
```
============================================================================
ANT-2026-D7STJUWL  [medium]  CWE-770  dos
Memory DoS in TIFF and EXIF IFD parsing via overlapping tag data
Location: src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:927  in ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()
Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6
============================================================================
```

A small, crafted image file can make Pillow use thousands of times its own size in memory while the file is only being opened, which lets anyone who can submit an image crash or stall the process handling it. A 144 KB TIFF makes `Image.open()` return normally while holding 1.6 GiB of memory. The largest such standard TIFF, about 786 KB, asks for roughly 48 GiB, which in practice gets the worker killed by the operating system. The file declares a 1×1 image, so the decompression-bomb check never triggers and no warning is raised. There is no memory corruption; the impact is denial of service.

The bug is in `ImageFileDirectory_v2.load()` in `src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py` (around line 927). For every directory entry whose value is stored elsewhere in the file, it reads that value into a new `bytes` object with `ImageFile._safe_read(fp, count * unit_size)` and keeps it in `_tagdata`. `_safe_read()` only checks that the bytes exist. Nothing limits the total read across entries, and nothing stops every entry from pointing at the same bytes. An attacker can therefore give each of N distinct private tags an offset and count that covers the whole file, at a cost of 12 bytes per entry. Memory grows as N × file size, which is quadratic in the file size, and BigTIFF removes the 65,535-entry ceiling.

The same loop parses EXIF data, so the problem reaches beyond TIFF:

* A 66 KB JPEG APP1 segment costs about 340 MiB inside `Image.open()` itself, via `_read_dpi_from_exif()`.
* A 96 KB PNG `eXIf` chunk costs 754 MiB on `getexif()` or `ImageOps.exif_transpose()`.

findings.title: Pillow: Heap buffer overflow saving TIFF with libtiff when tags override image size
findings.summary:
```
============================================================================
ANT-2026-CS7N494P  [high]  CWE-787  memory-safety
Heap buffer overflow saving TIFF with libtiff when tags override image size
Location: src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1035  in ImagingLibTiffEncode()
Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6
============================================================================
```

When Pillow saves an image as a compressed TIFF, size information taken from the image's metadata can make the encoder read past the end of a heap buffer. Someone who uploads an image can use this to get the server process's memory, including pointers, copied into the saved file, or to crash the process. When the metadata also enables TIFF "Predictor=2" compression, the encoder writes past the buffer instead, corrupting the heap and aborting the process. This affects applications that write TIFF through libtiff (any `compression=` other than raw) and either carry the source metadata across with `exif=im.getexif()` / `tiffinfo=`, or simply re-save a crafted palette TIFF with `Image.open(f).save(out, "TIFF")`, which inherits its compression and predictor from the upload.

In `TiffImagePlugin._save`'s libtiff branch, only `BitsPerSample` is pinned to the real image when the tag list for the encoder is built (`src/PIL/TiffImagePlugin.py:1955`). `ImageWidth`, `ImageLength` and `PlanarConfiguration` are set from `im.size` but are then overwritten by the `exif=`/`tiffinfo=` merge loop at `:1768-1772`. `SamplesPerPixel` is never set for single-band modes, so a value from the caller's tags or from the source TIFF's own IFD reaches `TIFFSetField`. `ImagingLibTiffEncode` then passes a row buffer sized from the actual image (`src/encode.c:291`) to `TIFFWriteScanline` (`src/libImaging/TiffDecode.c:1035`) with no check against `TIFFScanlineSize()`, and libtiff consumes a full scanline of the tag-described width from it.

findings.title: Hono: `mount()` and `app.mount()` can forward a path that bypasses middleware scoped inside the mount prefix
findings.summary:
### Summary

`mount()` and `app.mount()` remove the mount prefix from the request path and forward the rest to the mounted application. Two mistakes in that step let a crafted request reach a route of the mounted application that the outer application protects with path-scoped middleware, such as an authentication check on `/app/admin/*`. The outer application routes on the original path, so the middleware does not run.

### Details

1. **Dynamic prefix** (all affected versions): for a mount such as `/api/:tenant/*`, the prefix was removed by the length of the route pattern, not of the matched prefix. A request with a longer or shorter first segment is cut in the middle, so `/api/a/xxxxx/admin/secret` reaches the mounted application as `/admin/secret`.
2. **Re-normalization** (since 4.12.21): the forwarded path was built from the decoded request path and assigned to `url.pathname`, which turns a decoded backslash into `/` and collapses `..`. `/app/public%5C..%5Cadmin/secret` reaches the mounted application as `/admin/secret`.

The fix removes the prefix segment by segment from the raw pathname, using the matched parameter values for its length. Route patterns that cannot be handled safely now throw: duplicate parameter names and a wildcard inside the last segment such as `/assets*`. A trailing slash in an `app.mount()` prefix no longer removes an extra segment.

### Impact

An unauthenticated client can reach a route of a mounted application that the outer application protects with path-scoped middleware.

This affects applications that use `mount()` or `app.mount()` and rely on middleware registered on a sub-path inside the mount prefix for authentication or authorization.

### Workarounds

Register the authentication middleware inside the mounted application.

findings.title: Bringing Rust to the Pixel Baseband
findings.summary: Posted by Jiacheng Lu, Software Engineer, Google Pixel Team Google is continuously advancing the security of Pixel devices. We have been focusing on hardening the cellular baseband modem against exploitation. Recognizing the risks associated within the complex modem firmware, Pixel 9 shipped with mitigations against a range of memory-safety vulnerabilities. For Pixel 10, Google is advancing its proactive security measures further. Following our previous discussion on "Deploying Rust in Existing Firmware Codebases" , this post shares a concrete application: integrating a memory-safe Rust DNS(Domain Name System) parser into the modem firmware. The new Rust-based DNS parser significantly reduces our security risk by mitigating an entire class of vulnerabilities in a risky area, while also laying the foundation for broader adoption of memory-safe code in other areas. Here we share our experience of working on it, and hope it can inspire the use of more memory safe languages in low-level environments. Why Modem Memory Safety Can’t Wait In recent years, we have seen increasing interest in the cellular modem from attackers and security researchers. For example, Google's Project Zero gained remote code execution on Pixel modems over the Internet. Pixel modem has tens of Megabytes of executable code. Given the complexity and remote attack surface of the modem, other critical memory safety vulnerabilities may remain in the predominantly memory-unsafe firmware code. Why DNS? The DNS protocol is most commonly known in the context of browsers finding websites. With the evolution of cellular technology, modern cellular communications have migrated to digital data networks; consequently, even basic operations such as call forwarding rely on DNS services. DNS is a complex protocol and requires parsing of untrusted data, which can lead to vulnerabilities, particularly when implemented in a memory-unsafe language (example: CVE-2024-27227 ).
